"Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
Junlin WangHaozhe ChenAng LiRahul ChalamalaZhuang Liu[[[[
Abstract
Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team’s result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.
1Introduction
📷Figure 1:Sample small teams, not agents or one big team. (a) Three ways to spend the same agents. A verifier keeps the best solution. (b) Qwen3.8-27B on four tasks. Parallel agents (blue) flatten quickly, one big team (green) rises and falls with its size, and parallel teams of ten (orange) keep improving. Brackets give the gain of parallel teams over each baseline at the largest budget both reach.
Test-time compute lets a fixed pre-trained model do better by spending more computation at inference (Snell et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). An ideal method would turn more compute into better results steadily. We study tasks where a verifier can score every attempt and only the best solution matters. Many tasks for coding agents have this form (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025) because a scorer can check each attempt automatically and only the fastest kernel or the finished proof matters. On such tasks there are two common ways to spend more compute on agents. The first is best-of-N sampling, one of the strongest methods when a verifier is available (Chen et al., 2021; Cobbe et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022; Brown et al., 2024). It runs N independent agents and keeps the one with the highest score. Yet best-of-N over individual agents saturates quickly. In our experiments, 50 agents already reach 81% to 100% of the gain that 100 agents reach.The second way is to let more agents work together on the task as one team. Multi-agent systems split the work among agents with different roles (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023), and recent work grows such teams to hundreds or thousands of agents (Qian et al., 2025). A larger team does not give more samples to select from. It changes a single sample, and its score does not rise steadily with its size (Qian et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025). Large groups of people and of language models tend to converge on one solution and lose the diversity that exploration needs (Lazer and Friedman, 2007; Wu et al., 2019; Weng et al., 2025).Figure 2:Parallel teams beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks at 100 agents. Qwen3.8-27B parallel agents (blue) and parallel teams of ten (orange). Brackets give the teams’ gain at the largest budget both reach.
Each approach has one half of what we need. Best-of-N takes advantage of the variation across samples. A team lets its agents work together and reach better performance more efficiently. We introduce parallel agent teams, which combine the two by applying best-of-N to independent small teams of collaborating agents (Figure 1a). Each team is a small group of agents that share a forum. At the same budget of agents, parallel teams score higher than both parallel agents and one big team and keep improving as the budget grows (Figure 1b). Averaged over 12 tasks, parallel teams of ten score 10% higher than parallel agents at a total budget of 10 agents and 27% higher at a total budget of 100 agents. At 100 agents, ten teams of ten beat one team of 100 by 8% to 30%. At equal dollar cost, teams of a 27B model also beat the frontier model GPT-5.6-sol on 4 of 8 tasks.A simple statistical model of best-of-N explains why parallel small teams win. The expected best of several samples is the mean score of one sample plus a gain from variance, which grows with the number of samples the budget buys. Parallel agents collect the largest gain from variance because they draw the most samples, but each agent has a low mean. One big team has a high mean, but it is a single sample and wastes the gain from variance, and a larger team does not guarantee a higher mean. Parallel small teams balance the two. Each team has a much higher mean than an agent, and several teams still collect most of the gain from variance. They also keep improving as the budget grows. At a given budget they draw fewer samples than parallel agents because each team costs several agents, so their best-of-N curve is still on its steep early part, where each additional sample raises the best result the most.Collaboration raises the mean score of each sample, and sampling turns the variance across samples into gains. Parallel agent teams get both and keep improving where best-of-N over individual agents has saturated, offering a simple way to scale test-time compute further.
2Parallel Agent Teams
We first describe best-of-N sampling and how we measure it, and then agent teams. We then introduce parallel agent teams, which combine the two.
Best-of-N sampling.
We study tasks with a verifier that scores any candidate solution so that the best of several candidates can be found without human judgment. For a fixed model, drawing more independent responses and keeping the best steadily improves performance (Brown et al., 2024). Let X be the score of one sample, such as one agent, defined as the score of its best verified submission. We report the expected best of N independent samples:𝔼⁡[max1≤i≤N⁡Xi].(1)We estimate it from a pool of L runs by taking every subset of N runs and averaging its best score over all (LN) subsets. With the scores sorted as v(1)≤⋯≤v(L), this average is ∑i=NLv(i)​(i−1N−1)/(LN). One pool thus gives the whole curve from N=1 to N=L. Take five runs that score 2, 4, 5, 7 and 9. Their expected best is 5.4 for one run (the mean), 7.1 for two and 9 for all five.
Agent teams.
Instead of working alone, agents can work together as a team on the same task. Past work shows that such teams can produce better results than a single agent (Li et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). We mainly study flat teams, in which peers share progress through a common log or memory (Park et al., 2026; Qu et al., 2026). Each agent has its own sandbox and context but shares a forum where any agent can post and read notes at any time. There are no roles, no manager and no assigned work. A team’s score is the best verified submission of any member (Appendix E). Section 6 studies an alternative team architecture in which a manager assigns the work.
Parallel agent teams.
Parallel agent teams combine the two by applying best-of-N to independent teams (Figure 1a), so a sample is one team. We measure compute as a budget of B agents that each run for the same fixed time. It buys N=B/k teams of size k. Parallel agents (k=1) and one big team (k=B) are the two ends of this family, and parallel teams lie in between. We use teams of ten unless stated otherwise and study the team size in Section 3.1.Table 1:The 12 tasks. Higher is better for every metric.TaskBenchmarkDomainMetricDabic Gravity InversionEdgeBenchGeophysicspoints 0–100Borden Source InversionEdgeBenchHydrogeologypoints 0–100Graph Node ClassificationEdgeBenchMachine learningpoints 0–100Ad Placement OptimizationEdgeBenchHeuristic optimizationpoints 0–100Carleson FormalizationEdgeBenchMath formalizationpoints 0–100MoE Load BalanceMLS-BenchML systemsreward 0–1Active LearningMLS-BenchMachine learningreward 0–1Browser ExploitExploitBenchCybersecurityladder 0–16KDA Chunk ForwardKernelBenchGPU kernel optimization1/latencyKimi-Linear DecodeKernelBenchGPU kernel optimization1/latencySwinMLP BF16KernelBench-VerifiedGPU kernel optimizationspeedupMultiscale CantileverTopOptStructural designCref/C

3Parallel Small Teams Beat Both
Figure 3:Averaged over 12 tasks, parallel teams score higher and keep improving for longer. Qwen3.8-27B parallel agents (blue) and parallel teams of ten (orange). (a) Expected best score normalized by that of ten agents. The gap widens with the budget. (b) Parallel teams gain more from each added agent.

Setup.
We use 12 long-horizon optimization tasks from six benchmarks (ByteDance Seed, 2026; Lyu et al., 2026; Lee and Brumley, 2026; Elliot Arledge, 2026; Meta FAIR, 2026; Ouyang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). They span nine domains from GPU kernels to formal mathematics (Table 1). In each task an agent gets a description, a working environment and a scorer it can call and then improves its submission for 12 hours. Each agent runs in the Codex harness (OpenAI, 2025) inside its own sandbox. Our main model is Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026). Section 5 repeats the comparison with a stronger model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and Section 3.4 compares against GPT-5.6-sol (OpenAI, 2026). Each task has about 100 independent runs and 10 teams of ten, and four tasks also have single teams of 16 to 100 agents (Appendix D).
3.1Better than one big team
Figure 1b adds one team of B agents on the four tasks where we ran one big team. Its score rises at first but not steadily. From 64 to 100 agents it drops on all four tasks. At 100 agents, ten teams of ten beat one team of 100 on all four tasks by 8% to 30%, and on two tasks one team of 100 even scores below the best of 100 independent agents.Figure 4 holds the budget at 100 agents and varies the team size. The best size lies in between on every task. Ten teams of ten score highest on three tasks, and two teams of 50 on Graph Node Classification, where both reached the maximum score. Section 4 explains why both ends lose.Figure 4:At a fixed budget, the best team size lies in between. 100 Qwen3.8-27B agents form 100/k teams of size k. The ends are parallel agents (k=1; blue) and one big team (k=100; green).

3.2Better than parallel agents
Figure 2 compares parallel agents with parallel teams of ten on each task. At a budget of 50 agents, the best of five teams beats the best of 50 agents on 11 of 12 tasks. At 100 agents, the best of ten teams beats the best of 100 agents on 10 of 12 tasks (Table 4). The gains are largest where individual agents rarely succeed. On Carleson Formalization the best of 100 agents scores 19.0 out of 100 while the best team scores 54.8. Averaged over the 12 tasks, parallel teams score 10% higher than parallel agents at a total budget of 10 agents and 27% higher at 100 agents (Table 4). Parallel agents beat parallel teams only on Kimi-Linear Decode and, by a small margin, on Active Learning.
3.3Slower saturation than parallel agents
Parallel agents improve monotonically as compute grows because an extra sample can only raise the best score, but they saturate quickly. At 20 agents, each task has already reached 60% to 94% of the gain that about 100 agents bring. Parallel teams keep improving for longer (Figure 3b). From 10 to 20 agents each extra agent adds 1.27% to the score of parallel teams but only 0.64% to the score of parallel agents. The gap between the two methods therefore widens as the budget grows.
3.4Beating a frontier model
Figure 5:At equal cost, parallel teams of a 27B model overtake a frontier model. Qwen3.8-27B parallel agents (blue) and parallel teams of ten (orange), priced by GPU time, against GPT-5.6-sol agents (green), priced by tokens. The dotted line marks the price of one GPT-5.6-sol agent.
We also compare teams with GPT-5.6-sol at equal dollar cost (Figure 5). A Qwen3.8-27B team of ten costs about as much as one or two GPT-5.6-sol agents (Appendix J). On Carleson Formalization one GPT-5.6-sol agent beats one Qwen3.8-27B team, yet for the price of five GPT-5.6-sol agents, eight Qwen3.8-27B teams reach 52.0 against 47.9. Across the eight tasks with at least five GPT-5.6-sol runs, Qwen3.8-27B teams beat five GPT-5.6-sol agents at the same price on four. GPT-5.6-sol scores high but varies little from run to run. More GPT-5.6-sol runs therefore add little while the best of several Qwen3.8-27B teams keeps climbing.
4Why Do Parallel Teams Win?
Parallel teams beat both common approaches. They beat parallel agents although at the same budget they draw ten times fewer samples, since a team of ten costs ten agents. They beat one big team, which puts the whole budget into a single sample. A simple statistical model of best-of-N explains both results.
4.1A statistical model
Assume that the score X of one sample follows a normal distribution 𝒩⁡(μ,σ2) and that samples are independent. The expected best of N samples is then μ+σ​aN. Here aN is the expected maximum of N standard normal variables, and aN≈2​ln⁡N for large N (Fisher and Tippett, 1928; Gnedenko, 1943, Appendix A;). Now let each sample cost c agents so that a budget of B agents buys N=B/c samples. The expected best is thenV⁡(B)≈μ+σ​2​ln⁡(B/c).(2)The three numbers affect the curve at different rates. The mean μ adds the same amount at every budget. The standard deviation σ multiplies the gain from variance. This gain grows only as 2​ln⁡N. The cost c cuts the number of samples from B to B/c but lowers the gain from variance by only about σ​ln⁡c/2​ln⁡B. A tenfold cost therefore matters little once the budget is large. For teams of size k the cost is c=k, and the mean μk and standard deviation σk depend on k:Vk​(B)≈μk+σk​2​ln⁡(B/k).(3)The first term is the mean of one team and the second is the gain from variance when sampling B/k teams. Parallel agents (k=1) and one big team (k=B) are the two ends of this family.
4.2One big team wastes variance
Parallel sampling takes advantage of the variance of scores. By Equation 2, more samples raise the expected best by σ​2​ln⁡N, so performance scales with compute at a rate set by the standard deviation σ. Parallel agents and parallel teams both draw more samples as the budget grows and collect this gain. One big team wastes it. It is a single sample, so 2​ln⁡(B/k)=0 and its expected score is just its mean μB, whatever its standard deviation. A larger budget then helps one big team only if a larger team has a higher mean, and a larger team does not guarantee that. From 64 to 100 agents the mean of one team falls on all four tasks where we ran such teams (Section 3.1). One big team therefore loses to parallel teams, which raise the mean and still keep most of the gain from variance.
4.3Parallel teams balance mean and variance
Figure 6:How the mean, standard deviation and cost of a sample shape the best-of-N curve. Expected best score in the statistical model for four sampling methods. A higher mean shifts the curve up, a larger standard deviation makes it rise faster, and a higher cost delays its start.
Parallel teams balance the gain from the mean and the gain from variance. Parallel agents collect the largest gain from variance, but one agent has a low mean. A team of ten raises the mean but draws fewer samples and so gives up some gain from variance. By Equation 2, an expensive method (μ2,σ2) at cost c beats a cheap method (μ1,σ1) at cost 1 at budget B whenμ2+σ2​2​ln⁡(B/c)>μ1+σ1​2​ln⁡B.(4)With equal standard deviations, drawing B/c samples instead of B loses only about σ​ln⁡c/2​ln⁡B, and this loss shrinks as the budget grows. A higher mean counts in full at every budget. At a budget of 200, a mean gain of only 0.88​σ pays for a 10× cost. Figure 6 shows how the mean, standard deviation and cost each change the curve. A method at ten times the cost can still win through a higher mean or a higher standard deviation.
4.4Testing the statistical model
We now check the statistical model against our measurements. On Graph Node Classification, a team of ten scores 79.0 on average and an agent 52.1 (Table 2). With the agents’ standard deviation σ=11.8, the team’s mean is 2.3​σ higher. Equation 4 requires only 1.4​σ at a budget of 100 agents. Scores on this task and on Browser Exploit are close to normal, and the fitted normals predict the measured curves well (Figure 7).Table 2 extends the check to all 12 tasks. A team’s mean exceeds an agent’s by 0.5​σ to 4.4​σ on every task, and the statistical model predicts the sign of the teams’ gain at 100 agents on 9 of 12. It overestimates the best of many agents where agent scores are far from normal, as with the long lower tail of failed runs on Ad Placement Optimization (W=0.66) or the pile-up below a ceiling on KDA Chunk Forward (Appendix B). The statistical model also explains the frontier model’s flat curve: a high mean with a small standard deviation leaves little for parallel sampling to gain.Figure 7:The statistical model predicts the measured curves when scores are close to normal. Left of each task: score distributions of one Qwen3.8-27B agent (blue) and one team of ten (orange) with normal fits. Right: predicted (solid) and measured (dotted) expected best score.
Table 2:The statistical model on all 12 tasks. Mean μ and standard deviation σ of one Qwen3.8-27B agent and one team of ten. W is the Shapiro–Wilk statistic (Shapiro and Wilk, 1965), which equals 1 for a normal sample. Gain is the expected best of 10 teams over that of 100 agents. 4.5Fewer samples, steeper gains
The same statistical model explains why teams scale better. The best-of-N curve rises fastest at small N and flattens as N grows. At a given budget an expensive method has drawn few samples and still sits on the steep part of its curve while a cheap method is already on the flat part. Differentiating Equation 2 gives the return to one more agent of budget, σ/(B​2​ln⁡(B/c)). This return grows with the cost c. At 20 agents the statistical model gives a team of ten (N=2) a marginal return ln⁡20/ln⁡2≈2.1 times that of an agent (N=20) at equal standard deviation. The measured ratio is 1.27% to 0.64% (Figure 3b). Earlier work observes a trade-off between the quality and the quantity of samples at equal compute (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Our statistical model makes this trade-off precise for best-of-N.
5Other Ways to Spend Compute
Figure 8:Two agents for 6 hours beat one agent for 12 hours. Qwen3.8-27B on Graph Node Classification. (a) Expected best score against agent-hours. (b) A longer session barely shifts the score distribution, while a team of two at the same cost shifts it to the right.
(a) Expected best score at equal agent-hours(b) Score distributions and normal fitsEquation 4 applies to parallel sampling with any way of producing a sample. We use it to evaluate two other choices, a longer session for each agent and a different model.
Longer sessions.
Instead of forming a team we can let each agent work longer. A 12-hour agent costs as much as a team of two agents that each work 6 hours (Figure 8, Appendix G). Longer sessions barely raise the mean. On Graph Node Classification an agent’s mean score rises only from 52.0 at 6 hours to 52.7 at 12, in line with the slowdown of long agent sessions (Liu et al., 2026). By Equation 4, doubling the cost pays off at this budget only if the mean rises by about 3.4 points. The 12-hour agents therefore lose even to plain best-of-N over 6-hour agents. A team of two spends the same hours on two approaches, raises the mean by 5.4 points and beats both.

## Ai Phù Hợp Với Ngành Công Nghệ Thông Tin?

Ngành Công nghệ thông tin phù hợp với người yêu thích công nghệ, có tư duy logic, kiên trì giải quyết vấn đề và sẵn sàng tự học. Không nhất thiết phải biết lập trình trước khi vào đại học, nhưng học sinh nên có hứng thú tìm hiểu cách các hệ thống máy tính và ứng dụng hoạt động.

### Những Tố Chất Phù Hợp Với Ngành CNTT

Dưới đy là một số đặc điểm có thể giúp học sinh học tập và phát triển trong ngành. [...] Có nên học Công nghệ thông tin? Học CNTT có khó không? Đy là những băn khoăn phổ biến của học sinh THPT khi đứng trước lựa chọn ngành học. Công nghệ thông tin (CNTT) vẫn có nhiều hướng nghề nghiệp trong lĩnh vực phần mềm, dữ liệu, bảo mật và hệ thống máy tính. Tuy nhiên, ngành học này đòi hỏi khả năng tư duy logic, kiên trì thực hành và chủ động cập nhật kiến thức. Để quyết định có nên học CNTT, học sinh cần nhìn nhận thực tế thị trường việc làm, độ khó của chương trình và mức độ phù hợp với [...] Nên học Công nghệ thông tin nếu bạn yêu thích công nghệ, có khả năng tư duy logic và sẵn sàng dành thời gian học tập, thực hành lu dài. Ngành CNTT phù hợp với người muốn sử dụng máy tính và phần mềm để giải quyết vấn đề thực tế, không chỉ với những học sinh đã biết lập trình từ THPT.

Tuy nhiên, quyết định chọn ngành cần dựa trên sở thích, năng lực và mục tiêu nghề nghiệp thay vì kỳ vọng rằng học CNTT chắc chắn có thu nhập cao.

In recent months, artificial intelligence agents that can reason, plan and use external tools to accomplish multistep tasks have already reshaped computer coding, online shopping, dinner reservations and cyberattacks.

Robotics might be next.

Ken Goldberg, a UC Berkeley roboticist and professor of engineering, said new models make it possible for teams of AI agents to develop robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments and revise the code when something doesn’t work. [...] Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which specializes in logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the new methods earlier this year to analyze parcel sorting data and test updates to robot behavior. Tests showed an increased capacity of over 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot; the change is now deployed across 30% of the company’s U.S. fleet.
